title: The crafts that make a film
description: Film draws on nearly every other art plus technical skills: screenwriting, directing, acting, cinematography, design, music, sound and editing.

facts.text: Editing is trimming and piecing together lengths of film into a complete motion picture; the editor judges how long each shot should last.

title: The Great Train Robbery tells a story across places
description: Porter's 1903 film for Edison's company used 14 shots and cut between the telegraph operator and the bandits to show simultaneous action, a break from theater-like staging.

facts.text: Porter cut back and forth between the tied-up telegraph operator and the bandits on the train to show action happening at the same time in different places.

title: What a film editor does
description: The editor reviews the footage, chooses the best takes, orders them and trims each shot, turning a pile of takes into the film.

facts.text: A common saying holds that a film is made three times: when the script is written, when it is shot, and again in the editing.
A film editor reviews all the footage, selects the best takes of each shot and orders them, moving from a rough cut to a fine cut.
The terms editing, cutting and montage are often used interchangeably for the process of assembling a film.

title: From splicing film to editing software
description: Editors once cut and spliced celluloid on linear machines like the Moviola; since the 1990s nonlinear digital systems jump straight to any frame.

facts.text: For most of film history, editors physically cut and spliced celluloid on machines that ran footage from the start of a take to its end.
Iwan Serrurier's Moviola, a machine that lets an editor view film while editing, was adapted for film editing in 1924; it was upright, with a single screen.
Since the 1990s editors have used digital nonlinear systems such as Avid, working at a keyboard and jumping instantly to any point in the footage instead of scrolling through every frame.

title: Continuity editing: cuts you do not notice
description: Classical Hollywood's continuity or invisible editing matches direction, position and time from shot to shot so space and time seem unbroken.

facts.text: Continuity editing is a system of cutting that keeps narrative action continuous and clear by matching screen direction, position and time from shot to shot.
The dominant editing style of classical Hollywood, from the 1930s to the 1950s, is sometimes called invisible editing because its cuts are so unobtrusive.
Continuity editing supports the viewer's assumption that space and time run on unbroken from one shot to the next.

title: Match on action
description: Cutting in the middle of a movement and continuing it in the next shot links the shots smoothly, even joining places filmed apart.

facts.text: In a match on action, a movement begun in one shot is picked up where it left off in the next, linking the shots smoothly and reinforcing a sense of consistent space.
In his Biograph films of 1908 to 1913, D. W. Griffith matched action on cuts: a character walks into a doorway outdoors and, in the next shot, enters an interior set, joining places filmed apart.

title: The 180-degree rule
description: Keeping the camera on one side of the axis of action keeps characters on consistent sides of the frame; crossing it needs a reestablishing shot.

facts.text: The 180-degree rule keeps the camera on one side of the axis of action, an imaginary line between the two main elements of a scene, usually two characters.
Following the 180-degree rule keeps each character in a consistent area of the frame, so the left-right geography of the screen stays the same across cuts.
The 180-degree line is not usually crossed unless a reestablishing shot, showing the space again, smooths the change.
Editors can also break continuity on purpose to undermine the viewer's sense of the space.

title: The establishing shot
description: A distant framing that shows how a scene's people, objects and setting are laid out before closer shots begin.

facts.text: An establishing shot, usually a distant framing, shows the spatial relations among the important figures, objects and setting in a scene.

title: Shot, reverse shot
description: Conversations are built from alternating shots of each character, usually close-ups cut to the flow of the dialogue, which lets the editor shape the performances.

facts.text: Shot/reverse shot is two or more shots edited together that alternate between characters, typically in a conversation.
Shot/reverse shot editing uses the eyeline match to connect characters shown separately in close-ups, and its cuts usually follow the flow of the dialogue.
Keeping the camera on a speaker, or cutting to another character's reaction while the line is spoken, gives the same moment a different tone.
Editors trim the ends of shots to make an actor seem to jump in on another's line, or draw out a pause; viewers credit actors with much that comes from editing.

title: The eyeline match
description: A shot of someone looking off-screen followed by what they see; the direction of the look tells you where each person is.

facts.text: In an eyeline match, one shot shows a person looking off-screen in one direction and the next shows what they see; if the person looks left, the next shot implies the looker is off-screen right.

title: Crosscutting builds suspense
description: Alternating two lines of action in different places at once, with shots growing shorter, turns a chase or rescue into suspense.

facts.text: Crosscutting, or parallel editing, alternates shots of two or more lines of action happening in different places, usually at the same time, linking them.
D. W. Griffith became famous for crosscutting in the last-minute rides to the rescue that climax his films.
In The Girl and Her Trust (1912), Griffith cuts between robbers escaping with the heroine on a railroad pump car and the hero chasing them by train.
Intercutting the lines of action creates suspense, and shortening the shots as the chase goes on speeds up the pace; crosscutting became a foundation of film narrative.

title: The jump cut
description: Leaving out part of an action makes time visibly skip, breaking continuity on purpose; Breathless and the French New Wave made it famous.

facts.text: A jump cut leaves out part of an action, producing a visible break between shots and shrinking time in an obvious way.
Jean-Luc Godard's Breathless (1960) used jump cuts that left out parts of the action, and French New Wave films made jump cuts a hallmark of their style.
Jump cuts break with mainstream continuity storytelling and expose a film's artificiality; they can also suggest a character's restless thoughts.

title: The match cut
description: A cut between shots with matching shapes or colors links two things, as when a bone becomes a satellite in 2001: A Space Odyssey.

facts.text: A graphic match, or match cut, joins two shots with strongly similar compositions, such as shape or color, to smooth a transition or suggest a comparison.
In 2001: A Space Odyssey (1968), a man-ape tosses a bone into the air and a single cut turns it into an orbiting satellite, a famous match cut from prehistory to the space age.

title: The Kuleshov effect
description: Viewers read an actor's neutral face from the shot placed next to it, because they take the face to be looking at it.

facts.text: Lev Kuleshov (1899 to 1970) was a Soviet film theorist who taught that montage, the cutting and joining of shots, was the most important part of filmmaking.
Kuleshov showed an actor's neutral face followed by different shots, such as soup, a child or a corpse, and viewers read the face as hungry, tender or grieving.
A shot has two values: what it shows by itself, and what it gains when placed next to another shot.
Viewers take the face to be looking at what comes next; a 2024 study describes the sequence as a glance shot of the face followed by an object shot of what is seen.

title: How solid is the Kuleshov experiment?
description: The footage is lost and accounts differ, but a 2016 study found that some sort of Kuleshov effect does exist.

facts.text: The original footage of the experiment is lost, and tellings of it differ, even about which shots were used.
It is doubtful the experiment worked exactly as Kuleshov claimed: the actor's face came from an existing film and likely held an ambiguous expression.
After replications gave conflicting results, a 2016 study with 36 participants found that some sort of Kuleshov effect does exist.

title: Diegetic and non-diegetic sound
description: Diegetic sound comes from the story world and characters could hear it; non-diegetic sound, like most scores, is only for the audience.

facts.text: A film's diegesis is its story world: the objects, events, spaces and characters in it, including things the audience infers but never sees.
Diegetic sound, whether a voice, music or a sound effect, is presented as coming from a source within the film's world.
Non-diegetic sound comes from outside the film's world, as most background music does; only the audience hears it, not the characters.
Internal diegetic sound comes from inside a character's mind, such as their thoughts or sounds they imagine: part of the story world, but heard by no one else in the scene.

title: Foley: sounds made after filming
description: Foley artists perform footsteps and other action sounds in sync with the picture, a craft named after Universal's Jack Foley.

facts.text: A Foley artist creates sounds to accompany specific on-screen actions, such as a person walking, a sword fight or a creaking door.
In the first decades of talkies, microphones were designed mainly to pick up dialogue, so sound effects had to be added at a later step.
The craft is named after Jack Foley, who almost single-handedly developed it in the late 1920s at Universal, adding clapping, laughter and other sounds to Show Boat as the film ran in real time.
Foley artists work on a Foley stage full of props, such as shoes of all kinds, and watch the scene on a large screen so they can create the sounds in sync.
For Titanic, Foley artists made the crackle of frost with frozen lettuce.

title: The sound designer
description: Since Walter Murch's 1979 credit on Apocalypse Now, a sound designer can oversee a film's whole sound concept.

facts.text: In 1979 Francis Ford Coppola gave Walter Murch the credit Sound Designer for Apocalypse Now, the first use of that title in film.
As sound designer, Murch oversaw the film's overall sound concept, including dialogue, sound effects, Foley and the final mix.

title: The sound bridge
description: Letting sound run across a cut, early or late, links two scenes and smooths the transition in continuity editing.

facts.text: A sound bridge carries sound across a cut: the previous scene's sound continues briefly into the next, or the next scene's sound is heard before its image appears.
Sound bridges are one of the most common transitions in continuity editing, stressing the connection between the two scenes.
